## Introduction

A putter must arrive with a useful face orientation and velocity, then respond to contact with the ball. Its mass distribution influences both stages. A large moment of inertia can reduce the angular response to a specified impact impulse, while also increasing the torque needed for a specified angular acceleration before impact. Neither effect, by itself, establishes how accurately a golfer will deliver the face.

The intermediate-axis theorem offers a precise example of how inertia affects rotational perturbations. It concerns a **torque-free rigid body** spinning about a principal axis. A club held through a shaft and grip is a different mechanical system. Its response depends on applied forces and couples, support motion, shaft deformation, gravity, and the golfer's impedance and control. The theorem cannot simply be relabeled as extra grip effort or evidence for a particular putter architecture.

This article develops the free-body result, shows what the earlier numerical comparison actually establishes, and connects inertia to the forced stroke and collision. A central-spine layout remains a design hypothesis to evaluate. No measured advantage in face control, scoring, or muscle effort is established here.

## Background: Principal Axes and Rotational Stability

Use an orthonormal frame fixed in a rigid body, with origin at its center of mass $G$. Let $I_G$ be its inertia tensor, $\omega$ its angular velocity, and $\tau_G$ the **total external moment about $G$**, all expressed in that frame. Then

$$
I_G\dot\omega+\omega\times(I_G\omega)=\tau_G.
$$

For distinct positive principal moments $I_1<I_2<I_3$, choose the body axes to diagonalize $I_G$. With zero external moment, Euler's equations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_1\dot\omega_1&=(I_2-I_3)\omega_2\omega_3,\\
I_2\dot\omega_2&=(I_3-I_1)\omega_3\omega_1,\\
I_3\dot\omega_3&=(I_1-I_2)\omega_1\omega_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The reference spin $\omega=(0,\Omega,0)$ is an exact solution. For transverse perturbations $\eta=(\delta\omega_1,\delta\omega_3)^\top$, first-order dynamics give

$$
\dot\eta=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & (I_2-I_3)\Omega/I_1\\
(I_1-I_2)\Omega/I_3 & 0
\end{bmatrix}\eta.
$$

The second Euler equation has a product of two small transverse components and contributes no first-order change in $\omega_2$. The two transverse coefficients have the same sign, giving eigenvalues $\pm\sigma$, where

$$
\sigma=|\Omega|\sqrt{
\frac{(I_3-I_2)(I_2-I_1)}{I_1I_3}}.
$$

Thus a perturbation with a growing-mode component initially grows exponentially. This linear approximation ceases to describe large departures. Analogous linearizations about the minimum- and maximum-inertia axes have oscillatory transverse modes. They do **not** imply damping, attraction to the original orientation, or correction of a spin-rate error. Repeated principal moments require separate treatment; the strict three-distinct-moment statement cannot be applied unchanged.

The body-frame balance and free-spin perturbation argument are developed in [MIT's rigid-body dynamics notes, §2.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/6fe39e8d5ce4ce746ca256dfea665eda_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_2.pdf). Here the axes are labeled by **moments of inertia**, not simply by an object's longest, shortest and intermediate geometric dimensions.

### Note on Magnitude and Scaling

The gyroscopic moment $\omega\times I_G\omega$ scales quadratically when every angular-velocity component is scaled together. The linearized growth rate $\sigma$ instead scales with $|\Omega|$. Its effect over an interval of duration $T$ depends on the dimensionless product $\sigma T$, the initial perturbation and the model's validity over that interval. A small speed alone proves neither practical insignificance nor a measurable putting problem.

Moments have units **N·m**, not newtons. A force comparison needs a specified lever arm and direction. Furthermore,

$$
\omega^\top[\omega\times(I_G\omega)]=0.
$$

The gyroscopic term does no instantaneous rotational work. Inertia can redistribute rotational motion without dissipating energy; aligning an inertia tensor does not supply damping.

### Constrained vs. Free-Body Dynamics

For a rigid club with a resultant hand force $F_H$ and couple $\tau_H$ applied at $H$, its rotational balance about $G$ contains

$$
\tau_G=\tau_H+r_{H/G}\times F_H+\tau_{\rm other,G}.
$$

Uniform gravity acts through $G$ and has zero moment about that point, but it remains in translational balance. This does not make gravity irrelevant to a hand-held club: the support forces and their moment arms participate in the rotational response. A head considered separately receives forces and moments from the shaft.

The total applied moment is generally nonzero and can depend on motion. A free-body instability therefore does not establish a universal additional grip-torque requirement. Even the exact torque-free intermediate-axis reference spin needs no moment; its instability concerns perturbations. A specified constrained or feedback model must determine how those perturbations evolve and what reactions or commands result. [Peraire and Widnall's Euler-equation notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/16-07-dynamics-fall-2009/5e1d8699338146e5127080b880b906d6_MIT16_07F09_Lec28.pdf) distinguish the external-moment balance from the subsequent free-motion stability calculation.

## Changing Effective Rotation Axes in Golf Swings

### Shaft Deflection

Mass properties require an origin as well as axis directions. For rigid components temporarily locked into one assembly, the inertia about a common point $O$ is

$$
I_O=\sum_i\left[
R_i I_{G_i}R_i^\top+
m_i(\|r_i\|^2\mathbf1-r_ir_i^\top)
\right],
$$

where $r_i$ runs from $O$ to component center $G_i$, and $R_i$ maps component axes into the common frame. The parallel-axis terms cannot be omitted when the tensors have different origins. The tensor definition, origin translation and axis rotation are given in [MIT's inertia-tensor treatment, §2.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/6fe39e8d5ce4ce746ca256dfea665eda_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_2.pdf).

A deforming shaft is not a locked rigid assembly. Relative velocities, elastic energy, damping and coupling to head motion enter its equations. An instantaneous geometric inertia tensor may describe a mass distribution, but rotating and adding two tensors is not a complete flexible-club model. The appropriate refinement introduces deformation coordinates and their coupled dynamics.

### Off-Center Shaft Attachment

An offset attachment changes the moment of a transmitted force about the head's center. It does not by itself prove an unstable mode. For a **rigid body point** $O$ with prescribed acceleration $a_O$, expressed in body coordinates, the moment balance is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_O={}&I_O\dot\omega+\omega\times(I_O\omega)\\
&+m\,r_{G/O}\times a_O.
\end{aligned}
$$

This follows by substituting the acceleration of $G$ into the COM balance and translating inertia to $O$. A fixed pivot has $a_O=0$. A moving hand point generally does not. Gravity contributes $r_{G/O}\times m g_B$ to $\tau_O$, with $g_B$ expressed in the same body frame. Mixing a COM tensor with pivot moments or omitting support acceleration changes the problem.

### Non-Uniform Golfer-Applied Torques

At zero angular velocity, a rigid body's angular acceleration obeys $I_G\dot\omega=\tau_G$. A torque along a nonprincipal direction can produce acceleration with transverse components. This is inertial coupling, a dynamical effect, and it does not require a nonzero gyroscopic term.

For example, rotate $\operatorname{diag}(0.001,0.002,0.0025)\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ by $45^\circ$ about its third axis. Its first two diagonal entries become $0.0015$ and its product entry becomes $-0.0005$. A moment $(0.001,0,0)\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ gives acceleration $(0.75,0.25,0)\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$. This is a manufactured mapping, not an estimate for a putter.

Rotating the **coordinates** also rotates moment and acceleration components and leaves the physical result unchanged. Rotating a body's mass distribution relative to a fixed applied moment is a different experiment. Principal-axis coordinates always diagonalize a symmetric inertia tensor; writing fewer off-diagonal entries does not demonstrate improved equipment.

### What Would Establish an Unstable Stroke Mode? {#consequence-frequent-excursions-into-unstable-regions}

Define a nominal stroke, its support/actuator model, admissible perturbations and the output to be preserved. Linearize that complete model, propagate perturbations over the stroke, and evaluate delivered face/path changes. Instantaneous alignment with a head principal axis is insufficient. Shaft modes, grip stiffness, damping, feedback delay and changing support motion can all alter the result.

Compliance and damping differ. A spring supplies a displacement-dependent restoring moment; a viscous damper dissipates energy at a rate proportional to squared angular velocity. Finite muscle or grip stiffness is not a new exact holonomic constraint. Neither unmeasured subconscious corrections nor extra cognitive load can be inferred from an inertia table.

## Conventional Putter Design and Its Limitations

Declare clubhead axes at address: $x$ approximately face-normal, $y$ heel-toe and $z$ upward. The upward and face-normal axes are distinct. Their subsequent world directions change as the club rotates; sorted principal moments need not correspond to these named axes.

For a short collision, approximating the head as rigid and neglecting other significant impulses,

$$
I_G\,\Delta\omega=r\times P,
\qquad
\Delta\omega=I_G^{-1}(r\times P),
$$

where $P$ is the impulse **on the head** and $r$ runs from its center to contact. Orientation is treated as fixed over this idealized impulse. Significant shaft/hand impulses must be added. The scalar relation

$$
\Delta\omega_z=\frac{(r\times P)_z}{I_{zz}}
$$

holds for arbitrary impulses when $z$ is a principal axis. Otherwise the full inverse tensor generally couples the angular-impulse components. A physical single-axis constraint is another model, with reaction impulses and inertia about its declared axis.

For a fixed angular impulse about a decoupled axis, increasing that moment of inertia reduces the angular-velocity jump. This is an impact-response result, not “static stability.” Actual ball launch also depends on delivered face and velocity, contact location, impulse direction, friction and the collision model. This article supplies no universal commercial MOI range or scoring correlation.

## Central-Axis Spine Concept: Mass Concentration for Stability

A central-spine layout specifies where material is placed; it does not uniquely specify a center of mass, inertia tensor, principal-axis orientation or shaft attachment. Those quantities must be computed from a defined geometry/density distribution or measured. More than one mass distribution can have the same tensor.

There are at least three separate design questions: gravitational moment about a declared support axis, the forced torque-to-motion response before impact, and the impulse response at impact. Moving material can change all three. None is determined by the label “central spine.” A design can be tested for favorable values without assuming that it must outperform perimeter weighting.

## Quantitative Estimate of the Stability–MOI Tradeoff

### Hypothetical Inertia Spectra {#example-normalized-results}

The earlier article attributed the following numbers to a uniform volumetric-grid comparison, but supplied no reproducible geometry, material distribution or calculation. They are retained here **only as hypothetical spectra A and B**, not as verified CAD results or measurements of either architecture.

| Spectrum | $I_1$ (kg·m²) | $I_2$ (kg·m²) | $I_3$ (kg·m²) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0.00023 | 0.00113 | 0.00133 |
| B | 0.00023 | 0.00062 | 0.00072 |

### Units and Model Scope

The conversion is $1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}=10^7\ \mathrm{g\,cm^2}$, so $I_{3,A}=13{,}300\ \mathrm{g\,cm^2}$. These dimensional values are not normalized. Both triples are positive and satisfy the inertia triangle inequalities; that permits a mass-distribution realization in principle. It does not establish a particular head shape, common footprint, total mass, manufacturability or alignment with the golfer's stroke.

### Interpretation

The ratio $I_{3,B}/I_{3,A}=0.54135$ is a 45.9% reduction in the **largest principal moment**. Without the eigenvectors it cannot be called a reduction in vertical-axis MOI. The difference $I_3-I_2$ falls from $2\times10^{-4}$ to $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, but that difference alone is not a growth rate or performance measure.

### Growth Rate and the Comparison Condition {#stability-gain}

For the torque-free intermediate-axis calculation, let $\gamma=\sigma/|\Omega|$. Then

$$
\gamma_A=\sqrt{1800/3059}\approx0.76709,
\qquad
\gamma_B=\sqrt{65/276}\approx0.48529.
$$

At **equal spin rate**, B's growth rate is approximately 36.7% lower, not 50% lower. Both reference spins remain unstable. Uniformly scaling all three moments leaves $\gamma$ unchanged, showing why a dimensional inertia gap cannot by itself quantify this instability.

At **equal angular momentum magnitude** $L$ along the respective intermediate axes, the comparison changes:

$$
|\Omega|=L/I_2,
\qquad
\sigma=L\gamma/I_2.
$$

Now $\sigma_B/\sigma_A\approx1.15303$: B's rate is 15.3% higher. This reversal is not a claim that one condition represents putting. It demonstrates that a comparison must state what is held fixed. Measured stroke histories, forced dynamics and delivered outputs are still needed for an equipment conclusion.

## Practical Consequences for Putting Performance

### Potential Advantages to Test {#advantages}

For a prescribed motion, an aligned mass distribution may reduce a particular transverse moment requirement. For a prescribed disturbing moment, the response may differ. These are hypotheses about specified inputs and outputs; they should be tested under matched conditions rather than presented as established improvements in closure or consistency.

Gravity needs its own comparison. About a fixed pivot a scalar illustrative pendulum satisfies

$$
J\ddot\theta+b\dot\theta+mg\ell\sin\theta=\tau,
$$

with $\theta$ measured from downward vertical, $J>0$, and viscous damping $b\geq0$. Gravity provides restoring stiffness near $\theta=0$ and destabilizing stiffness near $\theta=\pi$, even though its moment is zero at both poses. With $b=0$ and $\tau=0$, total mechanical energy is conserved; a restoring moment alone does not damp oscillations.

For synthetic $m=0.35\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=0.02\ \mathrm m$ and $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, the maximum gravitational moment is $0.06867\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. A cross-inertia term with $I_{xy}=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and acceleration $5\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$ has magnitude $0.0005\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. Their magnitude ratio is 137.34 when the sine factor is one and zero when it is zero. Compare the same reference point and moment component. These assumed values do not establish universal gravity dominance, and taking angular velocity to zero does not also set angular acceleration to zero.

### Tradeoffs and Missing Quantities {#disadvantages}

Lower inertia reduces the moment needed for one specified acceleration but increases acceleration under one specified moment. Static gravitational balance about a shaft axis means a particular moment projection vanishes under stated conditions; it does not imply that the entire gravitational potential gradient vanishes, that a pose is attracting, or that all grip loads disappear. A design assessment must include those distinctions as well as impact response.

### Who Benefits?

This article cannot identify a beneficiary group from the available evidence. A useful comparison would measure or reconstruct the full mass properties, attachment and shaft properties, then test matched delivery/contact conditions and participant variability. Relevant outcomes include face orientation, path, speed, strike location and ball launch. A claim about reduced muscular effort needs a corresponding physiological or defensible model-based measurement, with its uncertainty and assumptions.

## Extension to Full-Swing Clubs

Higher speed can increase velocity-dependent terms, but it does not restore torque-free boundary conditions. Full-swing analysis must still include shaft dynamics, the hand wrench and moving support. A sequence of segment-speed peaks or head-axis alignments cannot establish the mechanism of energy transfer, an unstable mode or a stabilizing neural response.

## Conclusion

The intermediate-axis theorem explains a specific free-body perturbation mechanism. Putter design requires the additional steps that connect physical mass distribution to supported motion, delivered contact and collision response. The hypothetical spectra illustrate sensitivity to the comparison condition; they establish no superiority of a central-spine design. The useful research question is which measured design changes improve a declared delivery or impact outcome under a verified model and representative uncertainty.

## In Layman's Terms

A loose object in flight and a club supported by hands do not follow the same equations. A mass layout that changes one free-spin behavior might also change the torque required to move the club or its response to a mishit. Those effects must be evaluated together. “Balanced,” “easy to accelerate,” “resistant to impact twist” and “returns after a disturbance” describe different properties.

## Critics' Comments

The two governed critiques correctly question the leap from a free-body theorem to putter performance. Their earlier versions also made unsupported replacements: that low speed necessarily makes the effect negligible, or that gravity must dominate at every pose. The corrected critiques retain the boundary-condition concern and give the missing scaling and moment comparisons. Neither a claim nor its criticism becomes evidence merely by sounding mechanically plausible.

## Synthesis: The AffineDrift Context

For a declared mechanical and actuator model, an input-affine representation $\dot x=f_p(x)+B_p(x)u$ can expose how equipment parameters $p$ affect drift and actuation. Changing inertia can change both maps. Zero input is a specified intervention; it does not automatically remove gravity, passive grip/shaft forces, contact reactions or internal activation states.

A planar invariant set needs a dynamical condition. For a regular state constraint $h(x)=0$, tangency requires $Dh(x)f_p(x)=0$ on that set in the zero-input model, together with appropriate existence assumptions. An inertia tensor alone does not prove this condition. Local eigenvalues, finite-time perturbation growth and asymptotic Lyapunov exponents also answer different questions.

The connection to control is therefore concrete: specify geometry and mass properties, close the support and actuator equations, compute the relevant perturbation or impulse response, and compare the resulting delivery against observations. Co-contraction may alter finite impedance in a biological model; it is not automatically a change in an exact constraint Jacobian. These distinctions allow mechanical design and human control to be investigated together without treating either as already identified.
